body:
E-liquid bottles come in several sizes, and the best one is not always the largest. The right choice depends on the nicotine type and strength, the device you use, how often you vape, how you store liquid and what you pay per milliliter. A size that suits a heavy sub-ohm user can be a poor fit for someone with a small pod, and a bargain-looking large bottle can turn into waste if you cannot finish it before it ages. This guide explains the common sizes, what each suits, how to compare price per milliliter, how shortfills work, how to keep liquid fresh, how to carry it, worked examples and the mistakes to avoid. It is written for adults aged 21 and over. Nicotine is addictive, and nothing here is medical advice.

## Why bottle size matters
Size affects three things: how long a bottle lasts, what it costs per milliliter and how well it keeps. A small bottle is cheap to try and easy to carry, but costs more per milliliter. A large bottle is cheaper per milliliter, but ties up money, takes space and stays open longer, which can dull flavor. Matching size to your use lets you save without waste. See also [how to read an e-liquid label](/blog/how-to-read-an-e-liquid-label/) to confirm what a bottle really contains.

## 10 mL and 15 mL: samples and trials
Small bottles of 10 or 15 mL are useful for trying a flavor, for travel and for people who vape very little. They cost more per milliliter, but the total outlay is small, so you can try several flavors without commitment. Many brands sell sample sizes in a few flavors. If you are new to a brand, a small bottle is a sensible start.

## 30 mL: salts and pods
Thirty milliliters is the standard size for nicotine salts. Because salts are high strength and used in small pods, a 30 mL bottle lasts a long time: a typical pod user might take two to four weeks to finish one. They are also easy to carry and store, and they keep well. Many nicotine-salt flavors in our [vape juice](/shop/vape-juice/) range come in 30 mL bottles at around $12. See [nicotine salts vs freebase](/blog/nicotine-salts-vs-freebase/).

## 60 mL: balanced shortfills
Sixty milliliter bottles are common for freebase and for shortfill recipes. They suit regular users of small to mid-size tanks and mouth-to-lung devices that use freebase. A 60 mL shortfill often has room for a nicotine shot, if you choose to add one. They offer a middle path between price and freshness.

## 100 mL: tank users
Hundred-milliliter bottles are best for sub-ohm tanks, which burn through liquid. They usually offer the lowest price per milliliter, but only if you will use it before the best-by date. A heavy sub-ohm user may use 10 mL or more a day, so a 100 mL bottle lasts about ten days. A light user might take months, and then the saving is lost. See [sub-ohm vs mouth-to-lung](/blog/sub-ohm-vs-mouth-to-lung/).

## 120 mL and larger
Some brands sell even larger bottles. They are only worth it for very heavy users, and they require careful storage. If you are considering one, check that you can finish it within a reasonable time.

## Price per milliliter
Divide the price by the size to compare fairly. A 100 mL bottle at $12 costs 12 cents per mL, while a 30 mL at $12 costs 40 cents. That gap makes larger sizes attractive for heavy use of freebase. But salts are used in much smaller amounts, so a 30 mL bottle can last as long as a much larger freebase bottle. Compare cost per day, not just per milliliter. See [how to compare vape prices per puff](/blog/how-to-compare-vape-prices-per-puff/).

### A worked comparison
Suppose Alex uses a pod and takes about 1.5 mL of salt liquid a day. A 30 mL bottle at $12 lasts 20 days, costing $0.60 a day. Suppose Blake uses a sub-ohm tank and takes about 8 mL a day. A 100 mL bottle at $15 lasts about 12 days, costing $1.25 a day, and a 60 mL at $11 lasts about 7.5 days, costing about $1.47 a day. For Blake the 100 mL is the better value. For Alex, a 100 mL bottle would last more than two months and may age before it is finished. Each should choose the size that matches their use.

## Shortfills and nicotine shots
A shortfill is a bottle that contains less liquid than its capacity, so that you can add nicotine shots. A 100 mL bottle may hold 80 mL of liquid and have room for a 10 mL shot. If you do not add a shot, the liquid is nicotine-free. Always read the label to see what the bottle contains and what strength results if you add a shot. See [PG and VG ratios](/blog/pg-vg-ratio-explained/) for how additions affect the ratio, and take care with calculations.

## Freshness and storage
Large bottles stay open longer, so keep them cool and dark and use a smaller refill bottle for travel. Heat, light and air shorten life. Keep the cap tight, and store bottles upright. See [how to store e-liquid](/blog/how-to-store-e-liquid/) for details, and [e-liquid shelf life and expiry](/blog/e-liquid-shelf-life-and-expiry/). Check the best-by date, and use older bottles first.

### Decanting into a small bottle
For daily use, many people pour a small amount from a large bottle into a small, clearly labelled bottle. Use a bottle designed for liquid, label it with the contents and strength and keep it out of reach of children and pets. Do not use food or drink containers. Keep the original bottle for the label and warnings.

## Carrying liquid
For travel, small bottles under 3.4 ounces (100 mL) fit carry-on rules, in a clear bag. Pressure changes can cause leaks, so tighten caps and keep bottles upright in a sealed bag. See [traveling with vapes](/blog/traveling-with-vapes-airline-rules/) and [best vapes for travel](/blog/best-vapes-for-travel/).

## Which should you pick?
- **Salts in pods:** 30 mL.
- **Freebase in small tanks:** 60 mL.
- **Freebase in large tanks:** 100 mL.
- **Trying a new flavor:** 10 to 30 mL.
- **Traveling:** a small bottle.

If you are unsure of your hardware, our [first vape kit guide](/blog/first-vape-kit-guide/) can help. Adults 21+ only.

## Common mistakes
- **Buying a large bottle of an untried flavor.**
- **Ignoring the best-by date.**
- **Assuming a 100 mL bottle is all liquid.** Check for shortfill.
- **Comparing price per bottle instead of per milliliter or per day.**
- **Storing large bottles in warm places.**
- **Decanting into unlabelled containers.**

## Frequently asked questions in depth
### Is a bigger bottle always cheaper?
Per milliliter, usually. Per day, only if you use it before it ages.

### How long does liquid last once opened?
It depends on storage. Kept cool, dark and capped, liquid can stay good for months, but flavor fades over time.

### Can I use freebase in a pod?
Only if the maker says so. Pods are designed for salts.

### Do I need nicotine shots?
Only if you want nicotine in a shortfill. Many users buy ready-made bottles.

### Which size suits a beginner?
A 30 mL bottle of salt liquid in a flavor you like.

## Shop
Browse [vape juice](/shop/vape-juice/). Our product pages list size, strength and ratio, and options update the price. All products are for adults aged 21 and over, and nicotine is addictive.

## Bottle sizes and nicotine strength together
Size and strength interact. A 30 mL bottle at 50 mg/mL contains 1,500 mg of nicotine in total, and a 100 mL bottle at 3 mg/mL contains 300 mg. The large bottle holds more liquid but far less nicotine, which is why heavy tank users can go through a big bottle without taking in more than they would from a small salt bottle. This is also why you should never compare bottle sizes without checking strength. Read [nicotine strength guide](/blog/nicotine-strength-guide/) to see how mg/mL, percentage and volume fit together.

## Practical storage by size
Small bottles can live in a pocket or a bag, in a sealed pouch. Medium bottles suit a cupboard shelf. Large bottles are best kept in a closed cabinet, upright, away from the stove and the window. Whatever the size, keep every bottle out of reach of children and pets, with the child-resistant cap on. If you buy several bottles, label the date, and use the oldest first. A tidy shelf makes it easy to see what you have and to avoid buying more than you need.

## Sizes and the cost of waste
A bottle that goes stale is money lost. If you are not sure you will finish a large bottle, buy smaller ones. If you find you are always running out, step up. Many users settle on a size that lasts about a month, which is long enough to save money and short enough to stay fresh. Track how long each bottle lasts, and adjust your next purchase to match.

## Sizes and flavors
A 100 mL bottle of one flavor means a hundred milliliters of the same taste. If you like variety, two 60 mL bottles or three 30 mL bottles of different flavors may suit you better, even at a slightly higher price per milliliter. The best size is the one that you will finish while it still tastes good.

faq.q: What bottle size should I buy?
faq.a: 30 mL for salts in pods, 60 mL for freebase in small tanks and 100 mL for sub-ohm tanks, based on how fast you use liquid.

faq.q: Does a large bottle keep well?
faq.a: If stored cool, dark and capped, yes, but larger bottles stay open longer, so flavor can fade. Check the best-by date.

faq.q: Can I carry liquid on a plane?
faq.a: In containers of 3.4 ounces (100 mL) or less, in a clear bag, with caps tight.

faq.q: Should I buy a big bottle of a new flavor?
faq.a: No. Try a small bottle first.
